title: Four things that bring peace (III.23)
hookLine: do another's will, choose less, take the lowest place, want God's will
tomorrow: if God's gifts are good, why rest above them?

lines: THE WAY OF PEACE AND FREEDOM.
A LIST OF WAYS TO LOSE?
cards: A group project, a family vacation, a playlist for the car: somebody has to give way. Can losing that argument actually bring you peace? The Imitation says yes, and then it does something strange.

In chapter twenty-three of book three, Christ promises to teach the way of peace and true freedom. The disciple says, please, I love to hear it. And what comes next sounds less like peace than a list of ways to lose.

teach.h: ANOTHER'S WILL, LESS, THE LOWEST PLACE.
teach.b: Here's the list. Be eager to do another's will rather than your own. Choose always to have less rather than more.
Look for the lowest place, and be willing to be beneath everyone.
Wish always, and pray, that the will of God be fully done in you. Then the promise: whoever does this enters the borders of peace and rest.
So the puzzle: how do losing your way, owning less and sitting in the back add up to peace? Look at what each one lets go of.
The first loosens your grip on getting your way. The second, on having more. The third, on being seen.
And the fourth turns the other three around: the point isn't losing, it's God's will, in Latin voluntas Dei. A clenched hand gets tired. Every grip you loosen is one less thing to defend.
The disciple's reply holds the detail to tell a friend. This short word of yours, he says, holds much perfection: few words, full of meaning, rich in fruit.
And he admits that whenever he feels upset and weighed down, he finds he has drifted from this teaching.
That's the solution to the puzzle, in his own experience. The peace wasn't in winning. It was in not having to.

how: Catholics often read this chapter of the Imitation as a short rule for daily life, and some examine their day against it at night, asking where they held on and where they let go.

games.q: what does “four things that bring peace” mean?
o: four prayers to say before bed to sleep peacefully
four steps to win an argument without raising your voice
Christ's short rule: others' will, less, low place, God's will

p: the grip on getting your way
the will of God, fully done

s: the four things are about losing on purpose
they loosen grips, and the fourth points them all at God's will, not at losing.
the disciple calls it a short word full of meaning
few words, full of meaning, rich in fruit.
the disciple says he never strays from this teaching
he admits that when he's upset and weighed down, he has drifted from it.

games.q: your roommate wants the window open, you want it shut, and it's the third night of this. which of the four does the chapter put first?
o: be eager to do another's will rather than your own.
settle it by whoever has the better reason.
take turns, so each of you wins half the nights.
games.why: the chapter's first thing is another's will before yours. it isn't about who's right; it's one less grip to hold.

practice: Choose one of the four that will actually come up today: another's will, less, the lower place, or God's will. Picture the exact moment it will pinch, who's there and what you'll want to say.
Then decide now what you'll do instead, and rest in that plan for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Four things that bring peace. Christ's short rule in the Imitation: another's will, less, the lower place, and God's will done in you.
